passage: I'm Lakshmi, and last month our school cricket team lost the final by two runs. I sat on the boundary rope and cried into my knees; my throat felt tight. I had cared so much. After a while I wiped my face, walked over to Sangeeta, the other captain, and said, "Well played." She hugged me quickly. On the way home I thought about how slow I am running between the wickets. I didn't throw my bat or blame the umpire, though for one minute I wanted to. Next week I will practise my running.

qa.q: By how many runs did Lakshmi's team lose the final?
What was Lakshmi feeling as she sat crying on the boundary rope?
qa.a: Crushed: Lakshmi had cared so much, and the tight throat shows it.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt when Lakshmi said "Well played"?
qa.a: Probably appreciated, since she hugged Lakshmi quickly.

grounding: A child loses the final and is crushed, cries, congratulates the winners and decides what to practise.

passage:
"Siddharth, your Simran Bua knows how losing feels. I was eleven, captain of our school kabaddi team. We lost the district final by one point.
I was crushed. I wanted to throw my shoes at the referee and scream that he'd cheated. My chest was burning.
Instead I sat behind the stands and cried. Really cried. My coach sat with me and said, 'You're crying because you cared. That's good.'
Then I wiped my face and shook every hand on the winning team. 'Well played.'
That night I wrote down three things to practise. Next year, we won."

qa.q: By how many points did young Simran's team lose?
How did young Simran feel after the loss?
qa.a: She felt crushed and angry, her chest burning, wanting to throw her shoes at the referee.

qa.q: Which choice in the story shows the wise way to handle losing?
qa.a: Crying, then congratulating every winner and writing down three things to practise, instead of blaming the referee.

qa.q: How might the winning team have seen young Simran shaking their hands?
qa.a: They probably saw her as a good sport and respected her for it.

grounding: An aunt recalls losing a final and feeling crushed; she cried, congratulated the winners and planned what to practise instead of blaming the referee.

passage:
The inter-school quiz final had been delayed an hour by a power cut, and when it restarted, the buzzers kept sticking. Zubin's team lost to Ankita's by five points.
Zubin felt the loss like a punch. He had spent weeks learning capitals. He wanted to slam the broken buzzer and say it was the machine's fault.
Instead he went to the corridor and let a few tears fall.
Then he came back in and walked up to Ankita. "Well played. You knew the science round really well."
"Thanks," she said, surprised. "You guys were so fast on geography."
On the way home, Zubin wrote in his notebook: practise science.

qa.q: What delayed the quiz final by an hour?
How did Zubin feel after losing?
qa.a: He felt crushed, like he'd been punched, after weeks of learning capitals.

qa.q: What did Zubin do instead of blaming the buzzer?
qa.a: He let himself cry, congratulated Ankita, and wrote down what to practise.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Zubin congratulates her?
qa.a: Ankita seemed surprised and pleased, complimenting his team back.

grounding: A boy's team loses a quiz final and he is crushed; he cries, congratulates the winner and plans what to practise instead of blaming the buzzer.
